content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
The aim of the paper is to reduce the misclassifications of deep neural networks in a way that is energy efficient. Misclassifications in this paper are defined as adversarial and out-of-distribution samples, and natural errors (samples in training and test sets that are misclassified). A main target of the paper is to achieve that while saving energy (number of operations per sample). The proposed approach involves adding Relevant feature based Auxiliary Cells (RACs) after one or more hidden layer to decide, based on the detected features (class-specific), whether or not to end the classification early and declare the sample abnormal or output No Decision. By detecting the abnormal samples early on, the method can save unnecessary subsequent computation operations, and thus saving energy. The added RACs blocks use binary linear classificatiers trained on the relevant features for each class, and at test time they evaluate the activated features to dicide the corresponding class with a confidence score. If the RAC units disagree on their classification, the input sample is deemed abnormal and the classification is ended early. The main trick is where to place the RAC units, as if they are placed after the first layers, the features learned so far are not enough to distinguish the classes, and if they are placed immediately before the last layer, the high-level detected features will be useful but then there would be no chance to save energy.

First of all, the paper, especially the introduction, is not well written. The paper requires an unnecessarily high amount of time to grasp how the method works. The method is actually pretty simple. The problem under study is of relevance, as recent workshops on green ML at NIPS and ICLR have indicated. I find the proposed solution, however, quite heuristic. Why does it work? The paper does not shed light on this. 

There is a risk that the use of binary linear classifiers in RACs might end the classification immaturely, as the feature space might not (yet) be linearly separable and might still need more nonlinearities to classify it correctly. This is shown in the experimental results where the deeper nets with large number of classes have larger test error when RACs are used while the save in energy is not worth it (Figure 4). For a method that is proposed to reduce the natural errors, it's not clear how this serves the main target.

The hyperparameter tuning in the proposed method was dataset-specific, which affects the generality of the method aplicability.

Q.: For which other settings can RACs be put to good use?

Minor:  Note that the description of Figure 2 differs from the legends on the plots.

content.title: Authors' feedback
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their time and feedback. Our response to the comments are as follows:

1. We will rewrite the paper to make it more clear and concise. The revised version will be submitted by the deadline. 

2. To be clear on some defined terms:  Misclassifications are just natural errors i.e miss classified inputs from test data. Abnormal inputs are defined as adversarial, out-of-distribution and natural errors. 

3. Saving energy comes from early classification of easy examples and early detection of abnormal samples.

4. Regarding where to place RACs: If RACs are placed immediately before the last layer, not only there would be no chance to save energy but also there would be no chance to detect abnormal inputs. We observed that the RACs at layers just before last layers usually follow the final classifier’s decision. 

5. Why does it work?
If an example can be classified at early layers i.e. easy examples then processing it further by latter layers might lead to confusion and result in misclassification due to over-fitting. So, when RACs declare that an example is from class-k with high confidence then it is better to make an early classification. Also, we observed that the examples which are classified incorrectly do not have consistent hidden representations than the average correctly classified examples. If the decision from the two consecutive layers is different with very high confidence indicating confusion between these layers then there is a high probability for misclassification. Hence adding RACs and using their consensus to detect misclassifications can help in reducing test error. We will include this in the revised version of the paper. 

6. Use of binary linear classifiers at RACs: The main target is to improve the energy efficiency of the network at the same time being able to detect some of the natural errors. The test error with RACs is always better than the baseline design where test error indicates the percentage of misclassified examples by DNN with RACs. Note that no-decisions are not considered misclassification and hence is not included in computing test errors. We only desire to classify easy instances at RACs and so for these instance the relevant features obtained at RACs are good enough to be classified by a linear classifier. Some of the hard inputs might also be classified at RACs  which might still need more non-linearity to classify it correctly. This contributes to the non-zero false negative rate. However, the true positives are much higher than the false negatives.

7. Hyper-parameter tuning: We presented heuristic based techniques to tune the hyper-parameters. The results were presented for CIFAR10 dataset. However, it can be extended to any dataset. We agree that these hyperparameters are very dependent on the complexity of the network and dataset as mentioned in the paper. 
    a. Choice of validation layers: We start with adding RACs at the last two conv layer and measure the FNR on the validation dataset. We move the RACs toward the inner conv layers until the FNR value is within 5-10 %. We select a pair of earliest hidden layers as validation layers which result in the smallest false negative rate in the range of 5%-10%
    b. Number of relevant features k: We observed that k for a given layer is usually around 0.25 - 0.5 time the number of output channels (output filters) of that layer
    c. Confidence threshold: We have set this to 0.9 for cifar10 and 0.8 for cifar100 and tiny imagenet. We observed that the typical range of confidence threshold should be 0.8-0.9

8. For which other settings can RACs be put to good use: RACs are trained on class specific features and can be helpful for interpretability or explainability. They can help us in identifying if features specific to particular class are activated or not and so can potentially help in understanding the prediction made by the final classifier.

9. “Note that the description of Figure 2 differs from the legends on the plots.”:  addressed

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review:
I like this paper. It is well-written, easy to follow and it has a novel idea. The paper covers previous work of art well and introduces the problem. It explains the algorithm well through figures. 
My only concern is that the paper claims they are improving speed comparing to previous work, but they never compare their work to those mentioned and they don't talk about why there is no comparison provided with previous work of art. Particularly, the algorithm loses some accuracy while detecting adversarial and it is important to know how other algorithms do in a similar scenario.

content.title: Authors' feedback
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their time and feedback. Our response to the comments are as follows:
Our main focus is to be energy efficient while being able to detect some of the natural errors i.e. misclassifications from the test data. The natural error detection mechanisms proposed in literature claim to be better than the baseline detection mechanism [1] but they have additional energy requirements. We try to be at-least as good as baseline technique while being energy efficient i.e add robustness on top of energy efficiency. We try to use the linear classifiers introduced for conditional learning to detect errors by including relevant features concept. We observed that the baseline technique [1] is better than our technique in terms of detection rate by 10-20% but we have the advantage in terms of energy which other detection techniques don’t. 

1. Hendrycks & Gimpel (2017): This is a baseline technique which thresholds the output softmax value to detect natural errors. The baseline technique is better than the DNN with RACs in terms of detecting the natural errors. However, our technique offers energy efficiency on top of the detection ability. Comparing test error for iso accuracy and iso FNR:
       network, dataset   test error [1]   test error (ours)
a.   VGG16, CIFAR10          3.39                  4.48
b.   VGG16, CIFAR100       10.41                 13.73
c.   Res18,   CIFAR10          1.91                   3.2
d.   Res34,   CIFAR100        9.15                  12.18

2. Mandelbaum & Weinshall (2017): During test time, this method requires carrying over the embeddings of the training data and also the computation of the k nearest neighbors for each sample. This technique needs extra computation and memory than the baseline DNN.

3. Bahat et al. (2019): This technique claims to be better in terms of detecting natural error compared to baseline design and Mandelbaum & Weinshall (2017). Their results show that for CIFAR100 dataset,  AUROC with their technique is 0.864 while for the baseline technique it is 0.834. 
However they add MLP to detect natural errors and this MLP is trained on validation set. MLP used is a fully connected network with two hidden layers of width 30 each followed by RELU non-linearity and a batch normalization layer. For each image, they create ‘m’ transformed images,  pass it through the network and the resulting top N logits from original and transformed images are concatenated and fed to MLP.  	
This technique requires m times more energy for inference than the baseline design. 

References:
1. Dan Hendrycks and Kevin Gimpel. A baseline for detecting misclassified and out-of-distribution examples in neural networks. In International Conference on Learning Representations. 2017.
2. Amit Mandelbaum and Daphna Weinshall. Distance-based confidence score for neural network classifiers. In arXiv preprint arXiv:1709.09844. 2017.
3. Yuval Bahat, Michal Iranu, and Gregory Shakhnarovich. Natural and adversarial error detection using invariance to image transformations. In arXiv preprint arXiv:1902.00236v1. 2019.

content.title: Official Blind Review #4
content.review:
The authors introduce a mechanism for exiting the inference process early, without doing any more processing, if the network determines that there should be a classification early. The proposed mechanism is: learn separate linear classifiers on the outputs of layers in the convnet and use a decision rule based on agreement of these classifiers (and their confidences) in sequence, sometimes combined with the final output (described in Algorithm 3). 

The paper is poorly written (there are many simple grammar mistakes, the methods are not well motivated, and the methods are described in a confusing way), and more seriously the evaluation of the method is not complete. 

Details:

The evaluation is not complete. The threat model that the defense is evaluated under is not realistic: it assumes that the attacker does not have knowledge of the model: "we assume that the attacker has no knowledge about the detection mechanism but has complete knowledge about the baseline DNN (white-box attack with respect to baseline DNN)" (page 9). There are a number of mechanisms that are known that work well in this assumed threat model already, and other works have indicated why this is not a realistic threat model, see: [0]. As such the evaluation of adversarial robustness does not stand since there are no best effort, dynamic attacks on the defense presented. 

[0] https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.06705

content.title: Authors' feedback
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their time and feedback. Our response to the comments are as follows:
1. We will submit a revision by the deadline with proper motivation and will define the proposed method clearly.
2. Our main focus is to be energy efficient while being able to detect some of the natural errors i.e. misclassifications from the test data. We try to use the linear classifiers introduced for conditional learning to detect some of the errors by including relevant features concept. 
3. We have evaluated the adversarial robustness using zeros knowledge adversary [1] i.e. the attacker has no knowledge of the detector. Sorry for the confusion created by adding the term ‘white-box attack’. 

We have considered your review and have evaluated robustness of our method under full knowledge adversary using CW attack with L2 norm. These results will be updated in the revised version of the paper which will be submitted by the deadline. To generate the full knowledge adversaries, we have used targeted attack to fool the final classifier and RACs to predict same incorrect class. The full knowledge adversaries are constructed as:

	minimize [ l2_norm(x-xadv) + (c1 *(y_true - y_target))+ c2 RAC1_loss + c3 RAC2_loss] 

Where y_true is the logit value corresponding to true label of x and y_target is the logit value corresponding to the target label. Let ‘t’ be the targeted label
RAC1_loss =Σ [y_BLC1(j) - y_BLC1(t)]
RAC2_loss = Σ [y_BLC2(j) - y_BLC2(t)]
 y_BLCi(j) is the output of binary linear classifier corresponding to class j in RACi before applying sigmoid, t is the targeted class, c1, c2, c3 are penalty constants. 
[1] https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.07263.pdf

content.title: Reviewer response
content.comment: If you evaluate robustness with respect to the zero knowledge adversary, the robustness induced here is not significant (there are already a number of works that effectively defend in this regime).

content.title: Authors' response
content.comment:
Yes, we agree with that. Therefore we will be updating the paper with following results: 
Full knowledge adversaries are created by including the RACs' loss to the loss function that is optimized by CW attack . We will report the adversarial detection rate of DNN with RACs for full knowledge adversaries at mean adversarial distortion similar to zero knowledge adversaries. The zero knowledge adversaries are created such that the attack has (95-100)% success rate in fooling the final classifier of the DNN.

Dataset, network                 zero knowledge                             full knowledge
                                     adv TNR, mean l2 distortion         adv TNR, mean l2 distortion

a. CIFAR10, res18                    44.76, 1.38                                      9.10, 1.32
b. CIFAR100, res34                  43.49, 0.79                                      13.95, 0.73

As you mentioned, the adversarial robustness decreases in case of full knowledge attack.
However, our main goal is to decrease test error by detecting the natural errors in an energy efficient way. We evaluate the robustness towards adversarial and out-of-distribution examples to see if RACs work for other abnormal inputs. We agree that RACs are not very effective for detecting adversarial examples under full knowledge threat model but they are effective for detecting natural errors and out-of-distribution examples. we will make this clear in the revised version of the paper.
